title: Allergy Testing: Sensitization vs Allergy, Components and Tryptase
summary: Separate sensitization from allergy, choose skin or serum IgE testing, use peanut components to judge risk, time tryptase after anaphylaxis, and recognize unproven tests such as food IgG4 panels.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 56 Hits 1, 5, 8 and 11 and Traps 1, 2, 5 and 6 (first lesson for Ch. 56). Checked against Ansotegui 2020 (WAO), Beck 2019 and Schroeder & Cavacini 2010. Nuance: the Ara h 2 marker is region-dependent (Ara h 9 in the Mediterranean). Tryptase timing is taught from Beck 2019 (peak ~1–2 h, t½ ~2 h) rather than the reviewer’s 30 min–4 h window. Not taught as fact: IgE calibration and physical constants, FcεRI numbers, skin-test intradermal thresholds, hyper-IgE, α-gal, omalizumab ranges, class-switch signalling, mast-cell subtypes, lipid mediators, penicillin determinants, “8–10% of nonatopic children”.

objectives: Distinguish sensitization from clinical allergy and explain the limits of total IgE.
Choose between skin prick testing and serum specific IgE, including medication effects.
Interpret peanut component results and timed tryptase, and recognize unproven tests.

scenes.title: A panel full of positives
scenes.altText: Invented case: a 7-year-old with eczema has a large food-allergen IgE panel: peanut, wheat, soy and egg IgE all POSITIVE. The child eats peanut butter every week with no symptoms. A second, direct-to-consumer IgG4 panel lists “12 food intolerances”. The parents ask: “Must we remove all of these foods?” Question token: “What do these results actually show?”

cues.text: A 7-year-old with eczema has a large allergy panel: peanut, wheat, soy and egg IgE are all positive.
But the child eats peanut butter every week without any problem. A separate IgG4 panel lists twelve food intolerances.
Must the family remove all these foods? What do these results actually show?

props.label: What do these results actually show?

scenes.title: Sensitization is not allergy
scenes.altText: Mechanism card (Schroeder & Cavacini 2010): IgE binds with extremely high affinity to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils; allergen cross-linking triggers release of inflammatory mediators. Definition card (Ansotegui 2020, WAO): SENSITIZATION = allergen-specific IgE is present; ALLERGY = sensitization PLUS clinically relevant symptoms triggered by the culprit allergen. Total IgE card (Ansotegui 2020): the total IgE assay is nonspecific and gives only gross information; total IgE cannot be considered a reliable marker of allergy status.

cues.text: In immediate allergy, IgE sits on mast cells and basophils through a very high-affinity receptor. When allergen cross-links that IgE, the cells release their mediators.
Having allergen-specific IgE is called sensitization. Allergy means sensitization plus real symptoms when the person meets that allergen.
So a positive IgE test shows sensitization only. The clinical history decides whether it matters.
Total IgE is even less specific: it gives only gross information and is not a reliable marker of allergy.

props.label: Total IgE: nonspecific, not a reliable allergy marker

scenes.title: Skin test or serum IgE?
scenes.altText: Skin card (Ansotegui 2020): skin prick testing (SPT) remains the first-line approach in most instances; results are read against negative and positive controls, and the wheal size counted as positive depends on the device (≥ 3 mm for many devices). H1-antihistamines suppress SPT — most must be stopped 4–5 days, ideally 7, before testing; do not test on active dermatitis or severe dermographism; dermographism can cause false positives. Serum card (Ansotegui 2020): serum specific IgE (sIgE) is NOT affected by antihistamines, is not operator-dependent, and no allergen is given to the patient; results differ somewhat between reagents and manufacturers.

cues.text: Skin prick testing is still the first-line test in most cases. A drop of allergen is pricked into the skin and the wheal is compared with negative and positive controls.
What counts as positive depends on the device: for many devices, a wheal of 3 millimetres.
But antihistamines blunt skin tests, so most must be stopped four to five days, ideally a week, before. Skin tests also can’t be read on active eczema or severe dermographism.
Serum specific IgE avoids those problems: antihistamines do not affect it, it does not depend on the operator, and no allergen enters the patient. Results do vary between manufacturers.

scenes.title: Components, tryptase, and tests to avoid
scenes.altText: Component card (Ansotegui 2020): in the USA and Northern Europe, IgE to Ara h 2 is the best predictive marker for severe reactions to peanut (in the Mediterranean area, Ara h 9); Bet v 1 homologues (e.g. Ara h 8, “virtually innocuous”) and profilins are labile and typically cause local symptoms such as oral allergy syndrome. Tryptase card (Beck 2019): mast-cell tryptase rises steeply after onset, peaks ~1–2 h, half-life ~2 h, returns toward baseline within ~24 h; draw an acute sample plus a baseline ≥ 24 h later; consensus rise = peak > 1.2 × baseline + 2 μg/L; not raised in every anaphylaxis. Histamine has a very short half-life and needs prompt freezing. Unproven card (Ansotegui 2020): food-specific IgG/IgG4 panels — healthy people make IgG4 to commonly eaten foods; titres do not correlate with oral food challenges. Hook answer: positive IgE to tolerated foods is sensitization; the IgG4 panel is not a diagnostic test.

cues.text: Testing single allergen components sharpens the picture. In the United States and Northern Europe, IgE to Ara h 2 best predicts severe peanut reactions; Ara h 8 and profilins are fragile and mostly cause mild mouth symptoms.
After a suspected anaphylaxis, measure tryptase. It peaks about one to two hours after onset and has a half-life of about two hours, so draw early and again at baseline, at least 24 hours later.
A peak above 1.2 times baseline plus 2 micrograms per litre supports mast-cell activation. Histamine is gone too fast to be practical.
And avoid food IgG4 panels: healthy people make IgG4 to foods they eat, and it does not predict challenge results. For our child, the tolerated foods stay in the diet.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Positive peanut IgE = peanut allergy” (✓ sensitization only — history decides, and components such as Ara h 2 refine risk); “A negative skin test on antihistamines rules out allergy” (✓ antihistamines suppress skin tests; serum sIgE is unaffected); “IgG4 food panels identify food allergies” (✓ unproven — healthy people make food IgG4; it does not correlate with challenges).

cues.text: Trap one: positive peanut IgE means peanut allergy. No: it means sensitization. The history decides, and component testing such as Ara h 2 refines the risk.
Trap two: a negative skin test while on antihistamines rules out allergy. No: antihistamines suppress skin tests. Serum specific IgE is not affected.
Trap three: IgG4 food panels identify food allergies. No: healthy people make IgG4 to foods they eat, and it does not match challenge results.

scenes.title: “Could” vs “did”
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “IgE says the body COULD react; the history says it DID. Tryptase is the receipt — but only if you collect it within hours and keep a baseline copy.” Tokens: sIgE = could · history = did · tryptase 1–2 h + baseline. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: IgE says the body could react; the history says it did. Tryptase is the receipt, but only if you collect it within hours and keep a baseline copy.

Where it breaks: some component results, such as Ara h 2, do predict severe reactions better than others, and which component matters varies by region; tryptase is not raised in every anaphylaxis; and the oral food challenge, not any blood test, settles uncertain cases.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “sIgE = sensitization; allergy = sensitization + symptoms · total IgE nonspecific · SPT first-line but blocked by antihistamines; serum sIgE unaffected”, “Ara h 2 → severe peanut risk · tryptase peak 1–2 h, baseline ≥ 24 h · food IgG4 panels unproven”.

cues.text: Allergen-specific IgE shows sensitization, not allergy, so results are read against the history, refined with components such as Ara h 2, supported after reactions by timed tryptase, and never replaced by unproven IgG4 panels.

props.label: sIgE = sensitization · allergy = + symptoms · serum sIgE unaffected by antihistamines
Ara h 2 → severe risk · tryptase 1–2 h + baseline · IgG4 panels unproven

explanation.what: Plain language: an allergy blood or skin test shows that the immune system has made IgE to something — that is sensitization; whether it causes real reactions depends on what happens when the person meets it. Scientific terms: sensitization, allergy, specific IgE, total IgE, skin prick test, wheal, component-resolved diagnosis, Ara h 2, Ara h 8, profilin, oral allergy syndrome, mast-cell tryptase, baseline tryptase, IgG4.
explanation.why: IgE on mast cells must be cross-linked by enough allergen in a reactive tissue to cause symptoms, so sIgE presence alone does not predict reactions; IgE to some components (Ara h 2 in the USA and Northern Europe) is linked to severe peanut reactions, while labile proteins such as Bet v 1 homologues and profilins typically cause only local mouth symptoms. Tryptase released from activated mast cells is cleared over hours.
explanation.measure: SPT first-line (device-specific positive wheal, e.g. ≥ 3 mm; stop H1-antihistamines 4–7 days); serum sIgE unaffected by antihistamines (Ansotegui 2020). Tryptase: acute sample ~1–2 h after onset plus baseline ≥ 24 h; consensus rise > 1.2 × baseline + 2 μg/L (Beck 2019). Food IgG/IgG4 panels: unproven.
explanation.differs: Sensitization (sIgE present) vs allergy (sIgE + symptoms); SPT (suppressed by antihistamines) vs serum sIgE (unaffected); Ara h 2 (severe-reaction marker) vs Ara h 8/profilin (mostly local symptoms).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret a positive sIgE in a tolerant patient, choose serum sIgE for a patient on antihistamines or with extensive dermatitis, time a tryptase sample, and reject food IgG4 testing.

questions.stem: A child who eats egg daily without symptoms has a positive egg-specific IgE. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Sensitization without clinical allergy; keep the tolerated food
options.rationale: Correct. Allergy requires symptoms on exposure; tolerated foods need not be removed.

options.text: Egg allergy; remove egg from the diet
options.rationale: Incorrect. A positive sIgE alone shows sensitization only.

options.text: A laboratory error; IgE cannot be positive without symptoms
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sensitization without symptoms is common.

options.text: Confirm with an IgG4 egg panel
options.rationale: Incorrect. Food IgG4 testing is unproven.

questions.stem: A patient taking a daily H1-antihistamine cannot stop it. Which test best detects allergen-specific IgE?

options.rationale: Correct. Serum sIgE is not affected by antihistamines.
Incorrect. Antihistamines suppress the wheal and can give false negatives.
Incorrect. Total IgE is nonspecific and not a reliable allergy marker.
Incorrect. Unproven and not an IgE test.

questions.stem: A patient has suspected anaphylaxis during surgery. When should tryptase be collected?

options.text: About 1–2 hours after onset, with a baseline sample at least 24 hours later
options.rationale: Correct. Tryptase peaks ~1–2 h with t½ ~2 h; comparison with baseline (> 1.2 × baseline + 2 μg/L) supports mast-cell activation.

options.text: Three days later, once the patient is stable
options.rationale: Incorrect. By then tryptase has usually returned to baseline.

options.text: Only a single sample at any time
options.rationale: Incorrect. A baseline is needed to interpret the acute value.
